Analise o(s) documento(s) de cenário do projeto e gere o SRS completo no formato especificado, seguindo o processo de trabalho: buscas dedicadas na base de conhecimento para cada tipo de artefato, rastreabilidade validada entre os artefatos.

Documento(s) de cenário:
--- Project Scenario 3.pdf ---
IPG Job Manager
So the thing is, right now our grid users rely on Globus GRAM 
to run their jobs on remote machines across IPG, and honestly 
it just doesn't cut it anymore. People keep asking for things 
like being able to stage several sets of files at once, run 
more than one executable as part of the same submission, and 
actually look back at what happened with a job after the fact 
— none of that is really there today. We keep hearing 
complaints that there's no good history of executions, so when 
something goes wrong nobody can tell what happened or why. 
 
What I'm picturing is a Job Manager that lets users move and 
copy files between systems and kick off applications on 
whatever machine they're authorized to use, and they should be 
able to do this either through an API or from the command 
line, whichever fits their workflow. The core idea is a job 
made up of a main sequence of steps — file operations and 
execution operations chained together reliably — and then, if 
they want, an optional cleanup part that fires afterwards to 
delete temp files and directories whether the job succeeded or 
blew up halfway through. If something fails partway through 
the main sequence, I'd expect the system to stop, run the 
cleanup tied to whatever failed plus the cleanup for 
everything that already ran, going backwards, so we don't 
leave junk scattered across machines. 
 
It also needs to play nice with how the grid already handles 
security — there's a proxy/credential thing tied into the Grid 
Security Infrastructure that has to be respected, and only 
authorized users should ever be able to touch the systems on 
the list the Job Manager manages. And whatever we build, it 
has to keep some kind of resource list so people can only 
submit to machines that are actually registered, not just 
anywhere. 
 
On the people side, we've basically got two kinds of usage. 
Regular users will connect through the client side — find a 
server, submit a job, check on it, cancel it, look up old 
runs, that sort of thing. Then there's the admin side: someone 
has to install and keep the server itself running, someone 
manages the actual hardware and OS underneath it (might be the 
same person, might not), and there's also whoever takes care 
of the software repository server. Worth keeping in mind these 
admin folks need their own way to manage who has access, 
manage that resource list, browse jobs, and have some kind of 
log of what admin actions were taken. 
 
A couple of things I want to be upfront about not worrying 
about right now. Running one application split across two 
machines at the same time with them talking to each other — 
co-scheduling, that kind of multi-machine parallel execution — 
that's interesting but not something we need for this round. 
Same with building out a full workflow/DAG language with a GUI 
to draw out job flows, staging files in parallel instead of 
one at a time, juggling file permissions across different OS 
types when staging, or any kind of file caching to speed 
things up — all of that can wait, it's not critical for what 
we need delivered now. Also heads up, this version won't be a 
drop-in replacement for whatever the old Job Manager did 
before, so we'll need to help existing users transition rather 
than assume their old scripts just keep working. 
 
One more practical thing: whatever we ship needs to actually 
tell people when something breaks — a real error name, a 
message, and ideally the reason behind it, plus a way to log 
errors to a file users can point to themselves. And it should 
have some sense of timeouts so things don't just hang forever 
waiting on a response. 
 
One more thing since this is federal software built for NASA's 
IPG program, the whole thing has to meet Section 508 
accessibility requirements, not just some corner of it, so 
that's not something we can skip just because most of our 
users are pretty technical.

Sistema: IPG Job Manager

Resumo executivo: IPG Job Manager is a job orchestration service for NASA IPG grid users. It replaces limitations of Globus GRAM by enabling sequenced file operations and application executions on authorized registered resources, with optional cleanup, execution history, diagnostics, API and command-line access, and administrative controls.

Escopo: The system manages sequential jobs composed of file operations and application executions on authorized registered grid resources.
  Em escopo: Job submission through an API and command-line client
  Em escopo: Sequential file move, file copy, and application execution steps
  Em escopo: Multiple file sets and multiple executables in one job
  Em escopo: Optional cleanup after successful or failed execution
  Em escopo: Job status, cancellation, execution history, and error logging
  Em escopo: GSI proxy credential authentication and resource authorization
  Em escopo: Administrative access, resource, job browsing, and audit management
  Em escopo: Section 508 accessibility conformance
  Fora de escopo: Co-scheduling or parallel execution of one application across multiple communicating machines — excluded from this release
  Fora de escopo: Workflow/DAG language and graphical workflow editor — excluded from this release
  Fora de escopo: Parallel file staging — file operations are executed sequentially in this release
  Fora de escopo: Cross-operating-system file-permission management during staging — excluded from this release
  Fora de escopo: File caching — excluded from this release
  Fora de escopo: Drop-in compatibility with previous Job Manager scripts — explicitly not provided
  Premissa: PA-01: Registered resources expose the capabilities required to perform authorized file and application operations. [INFERRED]
  Premissa: PA-02: IPG provides Grid Security Infrastructure credentials for authorized users. [INFERRED]
  Premissa: PA-03: Migration guidance for users of previous Job Manager scripts will be defined outside this software scope. [TBD]
  Restrição: REST-01 (Security): Authentication and authorization must respect the existing Grid Security Infrastructure proxy/credential model.
  Restrição: REST-02 (Compliance): The delivered system must meet all applicable Section 508 accessibility requirements.
  Restrição: REST-03 (Interface): User operations must be available through both an API and a command-line client.

Stakeholders:
  STK-01 - Grid user (Usuário primário): Discover servers, submit and monitor jobs, cancel jobs, review prior executions, and receive actionable errors.
  STK-02 - Job Manager administrator (Usuário primário): Manage user access, registered resources, job records, and administrative audit records.
  STK-03 - Job Manager server administrator (Usuário secundário): Install, operate, and maintain the Job Manager server.
  STK-04 - Resource hardware and operating-system administrator (Stakeholder externo): Maintain the hardware and operating systems hosting registered resources.
  STK-05 - Software repository server administrator (Stakeholder externo): Operate the software repository server used by the environment.
  STK-06 - NASA IPG program (Stakeholder externo): Receive an accessible, controlled, and auditable job-management capability for the IPG program.

Regras de negócio:
  RN-001 - Authorized resource access: Only users authorized through the grid security model may access managed resources.
  RN-002 - Registered-resource submission: Jobs may be submitted only to resources included in the managed resource list.
  RN-003 - Sequential main execution: A job main sequence executes its file-operation and execution-operation steps in their defined order.
  RN-004 - Failure cleanup order: When a main-sequence step fails, main execution stops; cleanup for the failed step and cleanup for previously completed steps execute in reverse execution order.
  RN-005 - Completion cleanup: Defined cleanup operations execute after the main sequence whether the job succeeds or fails.
  RN-006 - Administrative accountability: Administrative access-management and resource-management actions must be attributable to the administrator who performed them.

Requisitos funcionais:

  RF-002 - API job submission: The system shall accept a job submission through its API. [Must have]
  RF-003 - Command-line job submission: The system shall accept a job submission through its command-line client. [Must have]
  RF-004 - Main-sequence definition: The system shall accept a job definition containing an ordered main sequence of steps. [Must have]
  RF-005 - File move operation: The system shall execute a defined file move operation between systems in a job step. [Must have]
  RF-006 - File copy operation: The system shall execute a defined file copy operation between systems in a job step. [Must have]
  RF-007 - Application execution: The system shall execute a defined application on the selected resource in a job step. [Must have]
  RF-008 - Multiple file sets: The system shall accept multiple file sets within one job submission. [Must have]
  RF-009 - Multiple executables: The system shall accept multiple application execution steps within one job submission. [Must have]
  RF-010 - Cleanup definition: The system shall accept an optional cleanup definition for a job step. [Must have]
  RF-011 - Successful-job cleanup: The system shall execute defined cleanup operations after successful completion of a job main sequence. [Must have]
  RF-012 - Failed-job cleanup: The system shall stop the main sequence and execute applicable cleanup operations in reverse order after a main-sequence step fails. [Must have]
  RF-013 - Job status query: The system shall return the current status of a submitted job. [Must have]
  RF-014 - Job cancellation: The system shall allow a grid user to cancel a submitted job. [Must have]
  RF-015 - Execution-history retrieval: The system shall provide a grid user with records of previous job executions. [Must have]
  RF-016 - Error diagnostics: The system shall report an error name, message, and reason when an operation fails. [Must have]
  RF-017 - User-designated error log: The system shall write reported errors to a file location designated by the user. [Must have]
  RF-018 - Operation timeout: The system shall terminate an operation when its configured timeout expires. [Must have]
  RF-019 - GSI proxy validation: The system shall validate the submitting user's Grid Security Infrastructure proxy credential before accepting a job request. [Must have]
  RF-020 - Resource authorization validation: The system shall verify that the submitting user is authorized for the selected resource before executing a job step. [Must have]
  RF-021 - Registered-resource validation: The system shall reject a job step whose selected resource is not in the managed resource list. [Must have]
  RF-022 - Access management: The system shall allow an administrator to manage user access to managed resources. [Must have]
  RF-023 - Resource-list management: The system shall allow an administrator to manage the list of registered resources. [Must have]
  RF-024 - Administrative job browsing: The system shall allow an administrator to browse submitted job records. [Must have]
  RF-025 - Administrative audit logging: The system shall record each administrative access-management and resource-management action in an audit log. [Must have]

  RNF-005 (Reliability) - The system shall invoke every applicable cleanup operation in the defined reverse order in 100% of injected main-sequence failure tests. | Métrica: 100% of applicable cleanup operations are invoked in reverse order across the failure-injection suite.

[TBD: define API contract] | Métrica: 100% pass rate for the supported-operation conformance suite on both interfaces.

  HU-005 - Como grid user, quero define cleanup operations, para remove temporary files and directories after my job finishes or fails

Casos de uso:
  UC-001 - Discover Job Manager server | Ator: Grid user
    1. The grid user requests server discovery.
    2. The system searches for available Job Manager servers.
    3. The system returns an available server identifier.
  UC-002 - Submit sequential job | Ator: Grid user
    1. The grid user submits an ordered job definition through the API or command-line client.
    2. The system validates the GSI proxy credential.
    3. The system validates the selected resource and user authorization.
    4. The system records and starts the main sequence in its defined order.
  UC-003 - Stage multiple file sets | Ator: Grid user
    1. The grid user submits a job containing multiple file sets.
    2. The system processes the first defined file operation.
    3. The system processes each subsequent file operation in sequence.
  UC-004 - Execute multiple applications | Ator: Grid user
    1. The grid user submits a job containing multiple execution steps.
    2. The system executes the first application step.
    3. The system executes each subsequent application step after the preceding step completes.
  UC-005 - Define cleanup operations | Ator: Grid user
    1. The grid user associates a cleanup operation with a job step.
    2. The system validates the cleanup definition.
    3. The system stores the cleanup definition with the job.
  UC-006 - Check job status | Ator: Grid user
    1. The grid user requests the status of a job.
    2. The system locates the job record.
    3. The system returns the current job status.
  UC-007 - Cancel job | Ator: Grid user
    1. The grid user requests cancellation of a job.
    2. The system validates access to the job.
    3. The system records cancellation and stops remaining main-sequence processing.
    4. The system starts applicable cleanup.
  UC-008 - Review execution history | Ator: Grid user
    1. The grid user requests prior execution records.
    2. The system retrieves accessible job history.
    3. The system returns execution records including recorded errors when present.
  UC-009 - Manage user resource access | Ator: Job Manager administrator
    1. The administrator selects a user and a registered resource.
    2. The administrator creates, changes, or removes an access assignment.
    3. The system updates the assignment.
    4. The system records the administrative action in the audit log.
  UC-010 - Manage registered resources | Ator: Job Manager administrator
    1. The administrator requests to add, modify, or remove a resource.
    2. The system validates the requested resource-list change.
    3. The system updates the managed resource list.
    4. The system records the administrative action in the audit log.
  UC-011 - Review administrative audit records | Ator: Job Manager administrator
    1. The administrator requests administrative audit records.
    2. The system retrieves the requested accessible audit records.
    3. The system returns the records.

Critérios de aceite:
  CA-001 - Dado a supported client is running and one Job Manager server is available, quando the grid user requests server discovery, então the system returns one available server identifier
  CA-002 - Dado a valid API job request is prepared, quando the client sends the request to the API, então the system returns a job identifier and an accepted status
  CA-003 - Dado a valid command-line job definition is prepared, quando the user runs the submission command, então the system returns a job identifier and an accepted status
  CA-004 - Dado a job definition contains three ordered main-sequence steps, quando the user submits the job, então the stored job record contains the same three steps in the submitted order
  CA-005 - Dado a job contains a valid file move step, quando the step executes, então the source file is absent and the destination file is present
  CA-006 - Dado a job contains a valid file copy step, quando the step executes, então the source and destination files are both present with identical content
  CA-007 - Dado a job contains an authorized application execution step on a registered resource, quando the step executes, então the system records the application's exit status in the job record
  CA-008 - Dado a job submission contains two file sets, quando the user submits the job, então the system records both file sets in the job definition
  CA-009 - Dado a job submission contains two application execution steps, quando the user submits the job, então the system records both execution steps in the defined sequence
  CA-010 - Dado a job step has a valid cleanup operation, quando the user submits the job, então the system stores the cleanup operation associated with that step
  CA-011 - Dado a successful job contains a cleanup operation that deletes a temporary directory, quando the main sequence completes successfully, então the temporary directory is absent after cleanup completes
  CA-012 - Dado a three-step job has cleanup definitions and its third main-sequence step fails, quando the failure occurs, então the system does not execute later main steps and invokes applicable cleanup in reverse order beginning with the failed step
  CA-013 - Dado an accessible submitted job exists, quando the grid user requests its status, então the system returns one current job status
  CA-014 - Dado an accessible job is executing, quando the grid user requests cancellation, então the system records a cancellation status and starts applicable cleanup
  CA-015 - Dado the grid user has two accessible completed job records, quando the user requests execution history, então the system returns both job records with their final statuses
  CA-016 - Dado a job operation fails, quando the system detects the failure, então the returned diagnostic contains a nonempty error name, message, and reason
  CA-017 - Dado the user designates a writable error-log file and a job operation fails, quando the system reports the failure, então the designated file contains the error name, message, and reason
  CA-018 - Dado an operation has a configured timeout of 10 seconds and does not respond, quando 10 seconds elapse, então the system terminates the operation and records a timeout error
  CA-019 - Dado a job request contains an expired GSI proxy credential, quando the user submits the request, então the system rejects the request before creating a job record
  CA-020 - Dado a user has a valid GSI proxy but lacks authorization for the selected resource, quando the system validates the job step, então the system prevents execution on that resource
  CA-021 - Dado a job step selects a resource absent from the managed resource list, quando the user submits the job, então the system rejects the job step and reports an error
  CA-022 - Dado an authenticated administrator selects a user and registered resource, quando the administrator grants access, então the system stores the access assignment for that user-resource pair
  CA-023 - Dado an authenticated administrator provides valid resource data, quando the administrator adds the resource, então the resource appears in the managed resource list
  CA-024 - Dado job records exist and an administrator is authenticated, quando the administrator requests job browsing, então the system returns the existing job records
  CA-025 - Dado an administrator changes a user-resource access assignment, quando the system completes the change, então the audit log contains the administrator identity, action type, affected user-resource pair, and timestamp

Glossário:
  API: Programmatic interface through which a client submits and manages jobs.
  Cleanup operation: An optional operation associated with a job step to remove temporary files or directories after job completion or failure.
  GSI proxy credential: Grid Security Infrastructure proxy or credential used to authenticate a grid user.
  Grid resource: A machine managed by the Job Manager on which authorized job operations may occur.
  Job: A submitted unit of work containing an ordered main sequence of file and application-execution steps and optional cleanup operations.
  Main sequence: The ordered set of job steps executed before cleanup operations.
  Managed resource list: The administrator-maintained list of grid resources eligible to receive job submissions.
  Section 508: United States federal accessibility requirements applicable to this NASA IPG software.

Base: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 §9.6 · IEEE 830-1998 §3 · Sommerville (2016, cap. 4)
O Documento de Especificação de Requisitos de Software (SRS) é o contrato técnico que descreve o 
que o sistema deve fazer e sob quais condições de qualidade. Ele serve de referência para 
desenvolvedores, testadores, gerentes e clientes durante todo o ciclo de vida do projeto.
1.1 Artefatos Obrigatórios e sua Ordem
Um SRS completo e formal deve conter os seguintes artefatos, nesta ordem:
• ESCOPO: Define o que está DENTRO e FORA do projeto. Evita scope creep.
• STAKEHOLDERS: Lista todos os envolvidos: quem usa, quem financia, quem é afetado.
• PREMISSAS E RESTRIÇÕES: Fatos assumidos como verdadeiros e limites impostos ao projeto.
• REGRAS DE NEGÓCIO (RN): Políticas, fórmulas e condições de negócio que existem independentemente 
do software.
• REQUISITOS FUNCIONAIS (RF): O que o sistema DEVE FAZER — comportamentos, serviços, respostas a 
entradas.
• REQUISITOS NÃO FUNCIONAIS (RNF): Como o sistema deve SER — atributos de qualidade 
quantificáveis.
• HISTÓRIAS DE USUÁRIO (HU): Necessidades na perspectiva do usuário: Como [perfil], quero [ação], para
[benefício].
• CASOS DE USO (UC): Interações detalhadas ator-sistema com fluxo principal, alternativo e exceções.
• CRITÉRIOS DE ACEITE (CA): Condições testáveis em formato BDD (Dado/Quando/Então) que definem 
quando o requisito está concluído.
• GLOSSÁRIO: Termos do domínio com definição precisa para eliminar ambiguidades.
1.2 Como os Artefatos se Interconectam
Os artefatos formam uma cadeia de rastreabilidade. Cada RF deve ter origem em um STK 
(stakeholder) ou RN. Cada HU deve ter pelo menos um RF associado. Cada RF e HU devem ter pelo menos um CA. Esta rastreabilidade garante que nada seja implementado sem justificativa de 
negócio e que tudo que foi prometido seja testável.
Cadeia de rastreabilidade mínima:
STK → (RN →) RF → HU → CA

4.1 Palavras Proibidas em Requisitos
As palavras abaixo indicam requisitos ambíguos, subjetivos ou não verificáveis. Quando 
encontradas, o requisito deve ser reescrito com métricas objetivas.
• rápido / veloz / ágil: Substituir por: 'tempo de resposta inferior a X ms/s'
• fácil / simples / intuitivo: Substituir por: métrica de usabilidade (ex.: task completion em < N min)
• amigável / bonito / moderno: Atributo subjetivo — vai para diretrizes de UI, não para RF/RNF
• eficiente: Substituir por: consumo de CPU < X%, throughput > Y req/s
• seguro: Substituir por: característica específica da ISO 25010 Security com métrica
• geralmente / normalmente: Indica exceções não documentadas — especificar todas as condições

When old requirements don’t exist
Most older systems do not have documented—let alone accurate—requirements. In the absence of 
reliable documentation, teams might reverse-engineer an understanding of what the system does 
from the user interfaces, code, and database. We think of this as “software archaeology.” To maximize 
the benefit from reverse engineering, the archaeology expedition should record what it learns in 
the form of requirements and design descriptions. Accumulating accurate information about certain 
portions of the current system positions the team to enhance a system with low risk, to replace a 
system without missing critical functionality, and to perform future enhancements efficiently. It halts 
the knowledge drain, so future maintainers better understand the changes that were just made.
If updating the requirements is overly burdensome, it will fall by the wayside as busy people rush 
on to the next change request. Obsolete requirements aren’t helpful for future enhancements. There’s 
a widespread fear in the software industry that writing documentation will consume too much time; 
the knee-jerk reaction is to neglect all opportunities to update requirements documentation. But 
what’s the cost if you don’t update the requirements and a future maintainer (perhaps you!) has to 
regenerate that information? The answer to this question will let you make a thoughtful business 
decision concerning whether to revise the requirements documentation when you change or 
re-create the software.
When the team performs additional enhancements and maintenance over time, it can extend 
these fractional knowledge representations, steadily improving the system documentation. The 
incremental cost of recording this newly found knowledge is small compared with the cost of 
someone having to rediscover it later on. Implementing enhancements almost always necessitates 
further requirements development, so add those new requirements to an existing requirements 
repository, if there is one. If you’re replacing an old system, you have an opportunity to document 
the requirements for the new one and to keep the requirements up to date with what you learn 
throughout the project. Try to leave the requirements in better shape than you found them.
Which requirements should you specify?
It’s not always worth taking the time to generate a complete set of requirements for an entire 
production system. Many options lie between the two extremes of continuing forever with no 
requirements documentation and reconstructing a perfect requirements set. Knowing why you’d like 
to have written requirements available lets you judge whether the cost of rebuilding all—or even 
part—of the specification is a sound investment.

information could be valuable the next time you need to modify the shopping cart function.

Enhancement and replacement

Most of this book describes requirements development as though you are beginning a new software 
or system development project, sometimes called a green-field project. However, many organizations 
devote much of their effort to enhancing or replacing existing information systems or building 
new releases of established commercial products. Most of the practices described in this book are 
appropriate for enhancement and replacement projects. This chapter provides specific suggestions as 
to which practices are most relevant and how to use them.
An enhancement project is one in which new capabilities are added to an existing system. 
Enhancement projects might also involve correcting defects, adding new reports, and modifying 
functionality to comply with revised business rules or needs.
A replacement (or reengineering) project replaces an existing application with a new custom-built 
system, a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) system, or a hybrid of those. Replacement projects are 
most commonly implemented to improve performance, cut costs (such as maintenance costs or 
license fees), take advantage of modern technologies, or meet regulatory requirements. If your 
replacement project will involve a COTS solution, the guidance presented in Chapter 22, “Packaged 
solution projects,” will also be helpful.
Replacement and enhancement projects face some particular requirements issues. The original 
developers who held all the critical information in their heads might be long gone. It’s tempting to 
claim that a small enhancement doesn’t warrant writing any requirements. Developers might believe 
that they don’t need detailed requirements if they are replacing an existing system’s functionality. 
The approaches described in this chapter can help you to deal with the challenges of enhancing or 
replacing an existing system to improve its ability to meet the organization’s current business needs.

2.3 Identificar, classificar e gerenciar documentos (L3)
Os documentos são outra fonte valiosa de requisitos. Eles são usados para transferir 
conceitos entre humanos ao longo do tempo e à distância.
2.3.1 Identificação e seleção de documentos como fontes de 
requisitos (L3)
Os tipos possíveis de documentos usados como fontes de requisitos são:
▪ Normas técnicas, legislação, regulamentos internos
▪ Documentos de requisitos (p. ex., de sistemas semelhantes ou do sistema a ser 
substituído)
▪ Manuais do usuário (p. ex., de sistemas concorrentes)
▪ Documentos de estratégia
▪ Documentação do objetivo
▪ Documentação do processo de negócio
Ao identificar documentos de forma pragmática, os engenheiros de requisitos usam seu 
conhecimento e experiência atuais do contexto (p. ex., domínio) para nomear documentos e 
tipos de documentos relevantes.
Durante a identificação sistemática de documentos, o Engenheiro de Requisitos define os 
objetivos da elicitação com um foco dedicado à identificação de documentos. Dois tipos 
diferentes de objetivos de elicitação devem ser considerados:
▪ Focado em informações: encontrar documentos para determinadas informações 
necessárias
▪ Focado em documentos: encontrar documentos de determinados tipos considerados 
relevantes para o desenvolvimento
Para a identificação sistemática de documentos, o Engenheiro de Requisitos pode:
▪ Pesquisar representantes de categorias típicas de documentos
▪ Pesquisar referências em documentos já identificados para outros documentos 
possivelmente relevantes
▪ Solicitar documentação relevante aos stakeholders já identificados
▪ Procurar documentação sobre sistemas relevantes já identificados (consulte 2.4)
Para decidir se um documento é relevante como fonte de requisitos ou não, o Engenheiro de 
Requisitos precisa estabelecer critérios específicos.

Level of detail
One of the biggest challenges is determining the appropriate level of detail at which to document 
requirements gleaned from the existing system. For enhancements, defining requirements for the 
new functionality alone might be sufficient. However, you will usually benefit from documenting all of 
the functionality that closely relates to the enhancement, to ensure that the change fits in seamlessly 
(region B in Figure 21-2). You might want to create business processes, user requirements, and/or 
functional requirements for those related areas. For example, let’s say you are adding a discount code 
feature to an existing shopping cart function, but you don’t have any documented requirements for 
the shopping cart. You might be tempted to write just a single user story: “As a customer, I need to be 
able to enter a discount code so I can get the cheapest price for the product.” However, this user story 
alone lacks context, so consider capturing other user stories about shopping cart operations. That 
information could be valuable the next time you need to modify the shopping cart function.
I worked with one team that was just beginning to develop the requirements for version 2 of 
a major product with embedded software. They hadn’t done a good job on the requirements for 
version 1, which was currently being implemented. The lead BA wondered, “Is it worth going back 
to improve the SRS for version 1?” The company anticipated that this product line would be a major 
revenue generator for at least 10 years. They also planned to reuse some of the core requirements 
in several spin-off products. In this case, it made sense to improve the requirements documentation 
for version 1 because it was the foundation for all subsequent development work in this product line. 
Had they been working on version 5.3 of a well-worn system that they expected to retire within a 
year, reconstructing a comprehensive set of requirements wouldn’t have been a wise investment.

Examine existing system interfaces to determine what 
data is exchanged between systems today. Understand how users use the current system. If no one 
understands the functionality and business rules behind the user interface, someone will need to look 
at the code or database to understand what’s going on. Analyze any documentation that does 
exist—design documents, help screens, user manuals, training materials—to identify requirements.
You might not need to specify functional requirements for the existing system at all, instead 
creating models to fill the information void. Swimlane diagrams can describe how users do their jobs 
with the system today. Context diagrams, data flow diagrams, and entity-relationship diagrams are 
also useful. You might create user requirements, specifying them only at a high level without filling 
in all of the details. Another way to begin closing the information gap is to create data dictionary 
entries when you add new data elements to the system and modify existing definitions. The test suite 
might be useful as an initial source of information to recover the software requirements, because tests 
represent an alternative view of requirements.CHAPTER 21 Enhancement and replacement projects 401
Sometimes “good enough” is enough
A third-party assessment of current business analysis practices in one organization revealed 
that their teams did a fairly good job of writing requirements for new projects, but they failed 
to update the requirements as the products evolved through a series of enhancement releases. 
The BAs did create requirements for each enhancement project. However, they did not merge 
all of those revisions back into the requirements baseline. The organization’s manager couldn’t 
think of a measurable benefit from keeping the existing documentation 100 percent updated 
to reflect the implemented systems. He assumed that his requirements always reflected only 
80 to 90 percent of the working software anyway, so there was little value in trying to perfect 
the requirements for an enhancement. This meant that future enhancement project teams 
would have to work with some uncertainty and close the gaps when needed, but that price was 
deemed acceptable.
Encouraging new system adoption
You’re bound to run into resistance when changing or replacing an existing system. People are 
naturally reluctant to change. Introducing a new feature that will make users’ jobs easier is a good 
thing. But users are accustomed to how the system works today, and you plan to modify that, which 
is not so good from the user’s point of view. The issue is even bigger when you’re replacing a system, 
because now you’re changing more than just a bit of functionality. You’re potentially changing the 
entire application’s look and feel, its menus, the operating environment, and possibly the user’s 
whole job. If you're a business analyst, project manager, or project sponsor, you have to anticipate the 
resistance and plan how you will overcome it, so the users will accept the new features or system.
An existing, established system is probably stable, fully integrated with surrounding systems, and 
well understood by users. A new system with all the same functionality might be none of these upon 
its initial release. Users might fear that the new system will disrupt their normal operations while 
they learn how to use it. Even worse, it might not support their current operations. Users might even 
be afraid of losing their jobs if the system automates tasks they perform manually today. It’s not 
uncommon to hear users say that they will accept the new system only if it does everything the old 
system does—even if they don’t personally use all of that functionality at present.
To mitigate the risk of user resistance, you first need to understand the business objectives and 
the user requirements. If either of these misses the mark, you will lose the users’ trust quickly.

GABARITO — Project Scenario 3: IPG Job Manager
Use: "ground_truth" field for RAGAS (context_precision / context_recall).
Each line is an atomic, checkable claim against the scenario text and the
knowledge base — not a full SRS, just the set of facts a well-grounded SRS
for this scenario should be able to cover.

- Users can move/copy files between systems and launch applications on authorized machines, via API or command line.
- A job consists of a main sequence of file and execution operations, executed reliably in order.
- An optional cleanup step can run after the main sequence, whether the job succeeded or failed.
- On failure partway through the main sequence, the system must run cleanup for the failed step and for all previously completed steps, in reverse order.
- The system must integrate with the existing Grid Security Infrastructure (GSI) proxy/credential mechanism.
- Only authorized users can access the systems the Job Manager manages.
- The system must maintain a resource list; users can only submit jobs to registered machines.
- Regular users interact through a client: find a server, submit a job, check on it, cancel it, look up old runs.
- Admin roles include: server installer/maintainer, hardware/OS manager, and software repository server manager.
- Admins need their own way to manage access, manage the resource list, browse jobs, and view a log of admin actions.
- Co-scheduling (running one application split across two machines simultaneously) is explicitly out of scope for this version.
- A full workflow/DAG language with a GUI is explicitly out of scope for this version.
- Parallel file staging, cross-OS file permission handling during staging, and file caching are explicitly out of scope for this version.
- This version is not a drop-in replacement for the old Job Manager; existing users need transition support.
- Error reporting must include a real error name, a message, and ideally the reason, plus file-based error logging.
- The system must implement timeouts so operations don't hang forever waiting on a response.
- As federal software built for NASA's IPG program, the whole system must meet Section 508 accessibility requirements.

fluxos_alternativos: 1a. The user omits cleanup for a step → the system accepts the step without cleanup.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. The cleanup definition is invalid → the system reports diagnostics and rejects that definition (ref. RF-016).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The grid user has submitted or may access the target job.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The current job status is returned.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No status is disclosed for an inaccessible or unknown job.
fluxo_principal: 1. The grid user requests the status of a job.
2. The system locates the job record.
3. The system returns the current job status.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. The job has completed → the system returns its final status.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. The job does not exist or is inaccessible → the system reports diagnostics (ref. RF-016).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The grid user may access the target submitted job.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The job cancellation is recorded and applicable cleanup is started.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The job remains unchanged when cancellation is not accepted.
fluxo_principal: 1. The grid user requests cancellation of a job.
2. The system validates access to the job.
3. The system records cancellation and stops remaining main-sequence processing.
4. The system starts applicable cleanup.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. The job is already complete → the system returns its final status without changing it.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. The user is not authorized for the job → the system rejects cancellation and reports diagnostics (ref. RN-001, RF-016).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The grid user has access to prior job records.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: Prior execution records and available error diagnostics are returned.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No records are disclosed for an inaccessible request.
fluxo_principal: 1. The grid user requests prior execution records.
2. The system retrieves accessible job history.
3. The system returns execution records including recorded errors when present.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. No execution record exists → the system returns an empty result.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. The history request is unauthorized → the system rejects it and reports diagnostics (ref. RN-001, RF-016).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The administrator is authenticated with administrative access.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The user-resource access assignment is updated and audit-recorded.
fluxo_principal: 1. The administrator selects a user and a registered resource.
2. The administrator creates, changes, or removes an access assignment.
3. The system updates the assignment.
4. The system records the administrative action in the audit log.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. The requested assignment already exists → the system reports the current assignment.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. The selected resource is not registered → the system rejects the change and reports diagnostics (ref. RN-002, RF-016).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The administrator is authenticated with administrative access.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The resource list is updated and the action is audit-recorded.
fluxo_principal: 1. The administrator requests to add, modify, or remove a resource.
2. The system validates the requested resource-list change.
3. The system updates the managed resource list.
4. The system records the administrative action in the audit log.
fluxos_alternativos: 1a. The administrator requests the current list → the system returns registered resources.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. The requested resource data is invalid → the system rejects the change and reports diagnostics (ref. RF-016).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The administrator is authenticated with administrative access.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No audit records are disclosed to an unauthorized requester.
fluxo_principal: 1. The administrator requests administrative audit records.
2. The system retrieves the requested accessible audit records.
3. The system returns the records.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. No record matches the request → the system returns an empty result.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. The requester lacks administrative access → the system rejects the request and reports diagnostics (ref. RN-001, RF-016).

Reverse-order cleanup on partial failure of the main sequence

Resource list (registered machines) and restriction of submission to those machines
Client for regular users (find server, submit, check, cancel, look up history)

stakeholders.descricao: Regular user (grid user) — connects through the client to submit, check, cancel jobs, and look up old runs.
Server installer/maintainer (admin) — installs and keeps the Job Manager server running.
Hardware/OS manager (admin) — manages the underlying hardware and operating system.
Software repository server manager (admin) — manages the software repository.

regras_de_negocio.descricao: A job consists of a main sequence of file and execution operations, executed reliably and in order.
An optional cleanup step can run after the main sequence, regardless of success or failure.
On partial failure of the main sequence, cleanup must run for the failed step and for all previously completed steps, in reverse order.
Users can only submit jobs to machines registered in the resource list.
Only authorized users (via GSI credential) can access the systems managed by the Job Manager.
This version is not a drop-in replacement for the old Job Manager — existing users need transition support, with no guarantee that old scripts keep working.

requisitos_funcionais.descricao: The system must allow users to move/copy files between systems.
The system must allow users to launch applications on machines they are authorized to use.
The system must allow these operations to be performed via API or via command line.
The system must execute a job's main sequence of file and execution operations reliably and in order.
The system must support an optional cleanup step that runs after the main sequence, on either job success or failure.
The system must, on partial failure of the main sequence, run cleanup for the failed step and for all previously completed steps, in reverse order.
The system must integrate with the existing Grid Security Infrastructure (GSI) proxy/credential mechanism.
The system must maintain a resource list of registered machines.
The system must restrict job submission to machines registered in the resource list.
The system must allow regular users to find an available server.
The system must allow regular users to submit a job.
The system must allow regular users to check the status of a submitted job.
The system must allow regular users to cancel a job.
The system must allow regular users to look up old job runs.
The system must allow admins to manage user access.
The system must allow admins to manage the resource list.
The system must allow admins to browse existing jobs.
The system must maintain a log of administrative actions taken.
The system must report errors with a real error name and a message, and ideally the reason.
The system must log errors to a file that the user can consult themselves.

requisitos_nao_funcionais.descricao: System operations must implement timeouts, so they don't hang indefinitely waiting for a response.

requisitos_nao_funcionais.descricao: The system must fully respect the Grid Security Infrastructure (GSI) proxy/credential mechanism to authorize access to managed resources.

requisitos_nao_funcionais.descricao: As federal software built for NASA's IPG program, the whole system — not just part of it — must meet Section 508 accessibility requirements.
Errors reported by the system must include a real error name, a message, and ideally the reason, and must be logged to a file accessible to the user.

historias_de_usuario.descricao: As a regular user, I want to move/copy files between systems and launch applications on authorized machines via API or command line, so that I can run my jobs in whatever way fits my workflow.
As a regular user, I want to submit a job with a main sequence and an optional cleanup step, so that temporary files are removed regardless of whether the job succeeds or fails.
As a regular user, I want to check, cancel, and look up old runs of my jobs, so that I can manage and audit my own work.
As a server installer/maintainer, I want to install and keep the server running, so that the Job Manager stays available.
As an admin, I want to manage user access and the resource list, so that only authorized users submit jobs to registered machines.
As an admin, I want to browse existing jobs and see a log of administrative actions, so that I can monitor usage and my own team's actions.
As a user, I want to receive clear error messages (name, message, reason) and have errors logged to a file, so that I can diagnose failures myself.

casos_de_uso.descricao: Submit and run job — a user submits a job (main sequence of file/execution operations), the system executes it reliably and runs cleanup afterward (success or failure), including reverse-order cleanup on partial failure.
Manage job status — a user checks, cancels, or looks up the history of a submitted job.
Manage access and resources (admin) — an admin manages user access and the list of registered machines.
Review admin log — an admin browses the log of administrative actions taken on the system.

criterios_de_aceite.descricao: Given a job that fails partway through the main sequence, when the failure occurs, then the system runs cleanup for the failed step and for all previously completed steps, in reverse order.
Given a user attempting to submit a job to an unregistered machine, when the submission is attempted, then the system rejects it.
Given an operation waiting for a response, when the timeout threshold is reached, then the system aborts the wait instead of hanging indefinitely.
Given any part of the system's interface, when it is evaluated for accessibility, then it complies with Section 508.
Given an error occurs during job execution, when it is reported, then the system provides a real error name, a message, and logs the error to a file accessible to the user.
